articles.headline: The hill I will die on: Cheques are still the best way to pay for things | Claire Jackson
articles.teaser: A debit card might be quicker and easier, but there are thrills big and small to be had from whipping out your chequebookIt often takes other people to identify your quirks. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. articles.headline: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial

What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis.

articles.headline: How to restore dignity to the world of work | Letters
articles.teaser: Colin Montgomery suggests that expectations should be properly managed. Plus letters from Paul Hartley, Hartley Dean and Peter ThorntonJohn Harris’s jeremiad about what the world of work has become (A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue, 22 November) put me in mind of the old joke: “How do I get to Dublin?” “Well, I wouldn’t start from here.” Because, as he concludes, there’s almost no chance of any government being able to even begin to relieve this situation quickly, short of putting an emergency brake on 40 years of neoliberalism. As if.I’d like to suggest a real starting point for the fightback against this seemingly interminable malaise that looks set to blight generations to come: namely, begin from somewhere grounded in properly managed expectations. Because arguably, that’s what underpins all of this: we’ve all been cynically inveigled into a bargain that can never be fulfilled.
articles.originalHeadline: How to restore dignity to the world of work  | Letters

articles.headline: Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care | Letters
articles.teaser: Willemina Rietsema, a GP, says no explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Carrie Eckersley thinks we need to consider the wider context in which symptoms developRegarding Huw Green’s article (How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?, 22 November), the body and the mind/brain have strong connections both ways. It is therefore not surprising that major psychological distress can lead to physical symptoms, and the other way around.However, as a GP, I would recommend being extremely careful about equating “otherwise unexplained symptoms” with psychosomatic illness. No explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet).
articles.originalHeadline: Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care | Letters

articles.headline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
articles.originalHeadline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
